endorsements.title: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for AI-Enabled Device Software Functions (final guidance)
endorsements.quote: In a little more detail, for each modification included in the description of modification section of a PCCP, the modification protocol should address four different areas. One, the relevant data management practices. Two, the retraining practices. Three, defining performance evaluation. And four, planned update procedures.

commentary.bottom_line: FDA final guidance on predetermined change control plans asks manufacturers to describe data management, retraining, performance evaluation, and update procedures for each planned modification. No study supplied here tests whether this documentation prevents modified models from being deployed without predefined methods, and no study documents how often that hazard occurs.

perspectives.view: No study in this map tests the practice, and none measures the hazard it targets. The recommendation rests on a single regulatory guidance document. Under GRADE conventions, expert or regulatory consensus does not count as evidence of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The FDA final guidance states that each modification protocol in a PCCP should address four areas: data management, retraining, performance evaluation, and update procedures. The guidance uses "should" language. Manufacturers seeking an authorized PCCP will likely treat the four areas as expected content, although the guidance itself does not show that the protocols improve device safety.

commentary.research_gap: Studies could compare devices authorized with detailed modification protocols against devices modified through new submissions, measuring post-update performance drift, adverse event reports, and recall rates. Audits of authorized PCCPs could also test whether documented procedures match what manufacturers actually do when they retrain and release updates.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients cannot tell from the current record whether documented performance evaluation plans include data drawn from their populations, and they may need to ask manufacturers directly how subgroup performance is checked after each update.
